title: Oval willow shopping basket
subtitle: A market basket with a fixed cane handle
excerpt: A traditional oval shopping basket in brown and buff willow, 40 cm long by 25 cm wide, 20 cm deep, with a fixed looped cane handle at each end. The oval base is made from a lashed-frame construction rather than a slath, which is the standard for oval baskets in the British tradition.
sourceNotes: British basket-making guild traditional pattern; oval lashed-frame construction documented in Charles Thatcher, Rural Crafts and Industries (1947), public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.
The thinner rods woven between the stakes to build up the sides of the basket.
A long diagonal cut at the base of a rod to give a pointed insertion tip. Cut with secateurs in one stroke.
A pointed steel spike used to open up the weave to insert new rods or to thread the border work.

content.text: An oval shopping basket uses a different base construction than a round basket. Instead of a crossed-stick slath, the oval base starts with a lashed rectangular frame of heavier rods: two long base sticks (the runners) that span the 40 cm length, with shorter cross-sticks lashed between them to set the 25 cm width. The side construction is identical to a round basket once the
are inserted. Intermediate level because the oval form requires even more attention to stake spacing than the round.
Base runners: 2 brown willow rods, 50 cm, 10 mm at butt. Base cross-sticks: 7 brown willow rods, 35 cm, 8 mm at butt. Stakes: 28 brown willow rods, 90 cm, 7 mm at butt.
: 100 buff willow rods, 1 to 1.2 m, 3 to 4 mm. Handle material: 2 thick willow or centre cane loops, 60 cm circumference, 12 mm diameter.

Lay the two runner rods parallel, 20 cm apart. Lash the seven cross-sticks between them at equal spacings using a long buff weaver in pairing weave. The lashing holds the cross-sticks at right angles to the runners and sets the base dimensions. Pairing across seven cross-sticks gives 14 pairing rounds across the base width.
on each stake and push stakes alongside each cross-stick and along the runners using the
to open the weave. 28 stakes total: two beside each cross-stick (one per side) and four in the curved end sections of the base.

Fold the stakes upright and weave a four-rod wale for three rounds to set the upset angle. Side with pairing weave in buff to 18 cm height. The oval form requires the stakes at the curved ends to be more tightly spaced than those on the long sides; check that they remain even and do not bunch as the siding progresses.

Before working the final wale, insert the two handle loops. Each loop is pushed down through the weave at the centre of each short end, to a depth of 8 cm. The ends of the loop sit either side of the central stake at that end. Once the final wale is woven over the loop base, the handle is locked in.

Weave three rounds of four-rod wale at the rim. Work a three-rod behind-two border: take each stake, kink at the rim, pass behind two stakes, in front of two, behind one, and tuck inside. This border is slightly more decorative than the simpler three-behind-one and produces a wider, flatter rim suited to a handled shopping basket.

attrs.symptom: The oval is pulling into a rounded shape
attrs.cause: The cross-sticks were not evenly spaced in the lashed frame.
attrs.fix: Check the base frame dimensions before inserting stakes. The lashed base should be 40 cm by 25 cm. If the frame is uneven, re-lash before proceeding.

attrs.symptom: The handle loop is wobbling after finishing
attrs.cause: The loop was not pushed deep enough into the weave.
attrs.fix: The handle loop base must go 8 cm into the weave. If the basket is already finished, use the bodkin to push the loop base deeper, inserting from inside the basket.
